units.name: Acadia National Park
units.description: Acadia National Park protects the natural beauty of the highest rocky headlands along the Atlantic coastline of the United States, an abundance of habitats, and a rich cultural heritage. At 4 million visits a year, it's one of the top 10 most-visited national parks in the United States. Visitors enjoy 27 miles of historic motor roads, 158 miles of hiking trails, and 45 miles of carriage roads.

attractions.name: Sieur de Monts Nature Center
attractions.description: Sieur de Monts Nature Center tells the story of natural history in the area.

attractions.name: Acadia Gateway Center
attractions.description: The Acadia Gateway Center is a new intermodal transit and welcome center that serves visitors to Downeast Maine and Acadia National Park. It is located on Route 3 in Trenton three miles north of Mount Desert Island. Visitor facilities include an Island Explorer bus stop, day-use parking, and an 11,000-square-foot welcome center with park and tourism information, Park Store, waiting area, and restrooms. The AGC will promote ridership on the Island Explorer from there and throughout the bus system and assist visitors in planning their trip to Downeast Maine. The National Park Service will staff the welcome center to provide visitors with a sense of arrival and orientation to the park, encourage use of the Island Explorer to visit the park, and ensure visitors have a park entrance pass and Cadillac Summit Road vehicle reservation. The AGC is owned by the State of Maine and operated by the Maine Department of Transportation in partnership with the National Park Service, Downeast Transportation Inc., and Maine Office of Tourism.

attractions.name: Jordan Pond Path
attractions.description: This shoreline loop circles Jordan Pond below surrounding mountains and the Bubbles. Forest sections include boardwalks, rocks, and footbridges; the western half is more difficult than the eastern half.

length.method: NPS Distance bullet: "Distance: 3.3 mile loop". Full pond circuit, not a one-way shore segment; no conversion.

attractions.accessibility: Uneven footing includes boardwalks, rocks, and footbridges. NPS warns that the western half can be challenging for people with mobility impairments.

attractions.name: Ship Harbor Trail
attractions.description: The route passes a narrow cove, rocky headland, spruce woods, and coastal bird habitat. Its two connected loops form a figure eight near the shore.

length.method: NPS introduction: "Ship Harbor Trail is a figure-8 trail covering 1.3 miles". Entire figure-eight route; no conversion or doubling.

attractions.accessibility: NPS calls the first loop ADA compliant. The second has occasional steps and plank trail. A drop at the trail entrance may require wheelchair assistance; trailhead vault toilets are not accessible.

history.event: President Woodrow Wilson created Sieur de Monts National Monument following land donations for federal protection.
Lafayette National Park was established, and George B. Dorr became its first superintendent.
The name Acadia National Park was adopted when Congress authorized acceptance of land on the Schoodic Peninsula.

units.description: Discover a landscape of contrasting colors, land forms, and textures unlike any other. The park has over 2,000 natural stone arches, hundreds of soaring pinnacles, massive rock fins, and giant balanced rocks. This red-rock wonderland will amaze you with its formations, refresh you with its trails, and inspire you with its sunsets.

units.name: Badlands National Park
units.description: The rugged beauty of the Badlands draws visitors from around the world. These striking geologic deposits contain one of the world’s richest fossil beds. Ancient horses and rhinos once roamed here. The park’s 244,000 acres protect an expanse of mixed-grass prairie where bison, bighorn sheep, prairie dogs, and black-footed ferrets live today.

units.name: Big Bend National Park
units.description: There is a place in Far West Texas where night skies are dark as coal and rivers carve temple-like canyons in ancient limestone. Here, at the end of the road, hundreds of bird species take refuge in a solitary mountain range surrounded by weather-beaten desert. Tenacious cactus bloom in sublime southwestern sun, and species diversity is the best in the country. This magical place is Big Bend...

units.name: Biscayne National Park
units.description: Within sight of Miami, yet worlds away, Biscayne protects a rare combination of aquamarine waters, emerald islands, and fish-bejeweled coral reefs. Evidence of 10,000 years of human history is here too; from prehistoric tribes to shipwrecks, and pineapple farmers to presidents. For many, the park is a boating, fishing, and diving destination, while others enjoy a warm breeze and peaceful scenery.

units.description: Hoodoos (irregular columns of rock) exist on every continent, but here is the largest concentration found anywhere on Earth. Situated along a high plateau at the top of the Grand Staircase, the park's high elevations include numerous life communities, fantastic dark skies, and geological wonders that defy description.

units.name: Canyonlands National Park
units.description: Canyonlands is a wilderness of canyons, buttes, and spires carved by the Colorado River and Green River. The park is divided into four distinct districts; no roads join them together. The districts share similar desert ecosystems, but each one provides unique opportunities for adventure and discovery.

attractions.name: Grand View Point Overlook and Trail
Neck Spring Trail
attractions.description: A walk back in time, this loop trail passes historic ranching features and two springs where cowboys watered cattle.

attractions.name: Chesler Park Viewpoint Trail
attractions.description: This popular trail leads to a pass overlooking a scenic expanse of desert grasses and shrubs surrounded by sandstone spires.

attractions.name: Big Spring Canyon to Wooden Shoe Canyon Loop Trail
Confluence Overlook Trail
attractions.description: Unlike other Needles hikes, this trail traverses dry, open country along the northern edge of the geologic faults that shaped the Needles. Trail ends at a cliff overlooking the junction of the Green and Colorado rivers 1,000 ft (304 m) below.

attractions.name: Big Spring Canyon to Elephant Canyon Loop Trail
Druid Arch Trail
attractions.description: This trail offers one of the most spectacular views in The Needles.

attractions.name: Chesler Park Loop and Joint Trail
attractions.description: This trail provides many great panoramas of the Needles formations. The Joint Trail winds through deep, narrow fractures in the rock.

units.name: Channel Islands National Park
units.description: Channel Islands National Park encompasses five remarkable islands and their ocean environment, preserving and protecting a wealth of natural and cultural resources. Isolation over thousands of years has created unique animals, plants, and archeological resources found nowhere else on Earth and helped preserve a place where visitors can experience coastal southern California as it once was.

units.name: Chiricahua National Park
units.description: Chiricahua National Park preserves towering rhyolite pinnacles, balanced rocks, and mountain landscapes shaped by volcanic forces in southeastern Arizona. Visitors explore scenic drives, hiking trails, and campgrounds beneath dark night skies. Rising between the Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts, the park supports diverse wildlife and protects a rich cultural history tied to Indigenous peoples, Apaches, Buffalo Soldiers, ranchers, and the Civilian Conservation Corps.

units.name: Congaree National Park
units.description: Astonishing biodiversity exists in Congaree National Park, the largest intact expanse of old growth bottomland hardwood forest remaining in the southeastern United States. Waters from the Congaree and Wateree Rivers sweep through the floodplain, carrying nutrients and sediments that nourish and rejuvenate this ecosystem and support the growth of national and state champion trees.

attractions.name: Boardwalk Loop
attractions.description: A boardwalk circuit introduces the park's floodplain landscape. A self-guided tour uses numbered stops to explain natural and cultural resources, and benches are shown on the route maps.

length.method: NPS Boardwalk Loop page: "The 2.6 mile boardwalk". Distance applies to the named boardwalk loop, using the page updated August 27, 2025; no conversion.

attractions.accessibility: NPS describes the boardwalk's flat surface as accessible. This is a physical description, not a current construction or flood-status check.

attractions.name: Weston Lake Trail
attractions.description: This trail follows Cedar Creek views and a cypress-tupelo slough with exposed cypress knees. Like other low floodplain trails, it is subject to periodic flooding.

length.method: NPS Weston Lake Trail (#3) entry: "Round Trip Distance: 4.5 miles". The page states mileages are approximate and assume all trails are passable; no conversion.

history.event: Commercial logging operations described in the park's floodplain history had ceased after extraction proved difficult and costly.
Congaree Swamp National Monument was authorized to protect the floodplain forest.
Congaree Swamp National Monument was redesignated Congaree National Park.

units.name: Crater Lake National Park
units.description: Crater Lake inspires awe. Native Americans witnessed its formation 7,700 years ago, when a violent eruption triggered the collapse of a tall peak. Scientists marvel at its purity—fed by rain and snow, it’s the deepest lake in the USA and one of the most pristine on Earth. Artists, photographers, and sightseers gaze in wonder at its blue water and stunning setting atop the Cascade Mountain Range.

units.name: Cuyahoga Valley National Park
units.description: Though a short distance from the urban areas of Cleveland and Akron, Cuyahoga Valley National Park seems worlds away. The park is a refuge for native plants and wildlife, and provides routes of discovery for visitors. The winding Cuyahoga River gives way to deep forests, rolling hills, and open farmlands. Walk or ride the Towpath Trail to follow the historic route of the Ohio & Erie Canal.

attractions.name: Brandywine Gorge Loop
attractions.description: From the falls trailhead, this loop descends into the gorge, crosses the creek on a footbridge, and returns by the falls viewing boardwalk. A lower viewing deck requires additional steps.
attractions.accessibility: The gorge loop is not wheelchair accessible: its unpaved surface is hilly and rocky in places. A separate short path reaches the upper boardwalk viewing area for wheelchair users.

conflicts.detail: The activity page gives 1.5 miles round trip; the park hiking table lists 1.4 miles.

attractions.name: Ledges Trail
attractions.description: The trail follows the Ledges rock formations and connects with other routes in the Virginia Kendall area. An overlook and the exposed Sharon Conglomerate are features of this landscape.
attractions.accessibility: NPS states that the trail is not accessible to visitors with mobility impairments.

conflicts.detail: The dedicated page describes 1.8 miles around the formations; the hiking table lists 2.2 miles, with unresolved route scope.

history.event: Enabling legislation authorized Cuyahoga Valley National Recreation Area under Public Law 93-555.
Name-change legislation redesignated the recreation area as Cuyahoga Valley National Park under Public Law 106-291.

units.name: Death Valley National Park
units.description: In this below-sea-level basin, steady drought and record summer heat make Death Valley a land of extremes. Yet, each extreme has a striking contrast. Towering peaks are frosted with winter snow. Rare rainstorms bring vast fields of wildflowers. Lush oases harbor tiny fish and refuge for wildlife and humans. Despite its morbid name, a great diversity of life thrives in Death Valley.

units.name: Dry Tortugas National Park
units.description: Almost 70 miles (113 km) west of Key West lies the remote Dry Tortugas National Park. This 100-square mile park is mostly open water with seven small islands. Accessible only by boat or seaplane, the park is known the world over as the home of magnificent Fort Jefferson, picturesque blue waters, superlative coral reefs and marine life, and the vast assortment of bird life that frequents the area.

units.name: Everglades National Park
units.description: Established in 1947 as the first national park created for its biodiversity, Everglades National Park protects 1.5 million acres of wetland, forest, and marine habitats and the native plants and animals that call it home. With several international designations, the park provides a major source of drinking water for local residents of South Florida and recreational opportunities for all.

units.name: Grand Canyon National Park
units.description: Entirely within the state of Arizona, the park encompasses 278 miles (447 km) of the Colorado River and adjacent uplands. Located on the ancestral homelands of 11 present day Tribal Communities, Grand Canyon is one of the most spectacular examples of erosion anywhere in the world—a mile deep canyon unmatched in the incomparable vistas it offers visitors from both north and south rims.

attractions.name: Park Store at the Visitor Center - Grand Canyon Conservancy
attractions.description: The Park Store at the South Rim Visitor Center features a wide variety of books, maps, apparel, souvenirs, and gifts to help you plan or remember your trip to Grand Canyon, and to learn more about its geology, ecology, and history. Purchases help fund new exhibits, scientific research, trail restoration, wildlife monitoring, ecological restoration, support for the arts, Junior Ranger and education programs, and historic building preservation.

units.name: Guadalupe Mountains National Park
units.description: Come experience mountains and canyons, desert and dunes, night skies and spectacular vistas within a place unlike any other. Guadalupe Mountains National Park protects the world's most extensive Permian fossil reef, the four highest peaks in Texas, an environmentally diverse collection of flora and fauna, and the stories of lives shaped through conflict, cooperation and survival.

attractions.name: Smith Spring Trail Loop
attractions.description: From Frijole Ranch, the loop passes Manzanita Spring and climbs toward the shaded vegetation around Smith Spring. The route offers views across the surrounding foothills and desert.

length.method: NPS overview: "Distance: 2.3 miles (3.7 km) round-trip, loop". Full loop from Frijole Ranch; no conversion or doubling.

attractions.accessibility: The section from Frijole Ranch to Manzanita Spring is paved. Beyond Manzanita Spring, the trail has loose or hardened rock surfaces; this does not establish accessibility of the full loop.

attractions.name: McKittrick Canyon Nature Trail
attractions.description: This short loop passes an intermittent seep, climbs a sunny slope, and returns on a less exposed slope. Exhibits explain desert plants, wildland fire, and Permian reef geology.

length.method: NPS overview: "Distance: 0.9 miles (1.4 km) round-trip, loop". Entire nature-trail loop, distinct from longer McKittrick Canyon hikes; no conversion.

attractions.accessibility: NPS describes loose or hardened rock surfaces with variable trail width. Accessible trailhead parking is not evidence that the trail itself is wheelchair accessible.

history.event: An early landowner began advocating national park status for the Guadalupe Mountains.
Guadalupe Mountains National Park was formally established, six years after congressional authorization.

Known for its striking plant and bird diversity, it's easy to find inspiration throughout the park’s 16,000 acres.

units.name: Kenai Fjords National Park
units.description: At the edge of the Kenai Peninsula lies a land where the ice age lingers. Nearly 40 glaciers flow from the Harding Icefield, Kenai Fjords' crowning feature. Wildlife thrives in icy waters and lush forests around this expanse of ice. Native Alutiiq relied on these resources to nurture a life entwined with the sea. Today, shrinking glaciers bear witness to the effects of our changing climate.

units.name: Kobuk Valley National Park
units.description: Caribou, sand dunes, the Kobuk River, Onion Portage - just some of the facets of Kobuk Valley National Park. Thousands of caribou migrate through, their tracks crisscrossing sculpted dunes. The Kobuk River is an ancient and current corridor for people and wildlife. For 9000 years, people came to Onion Portage to harvest caribou as they swam the river. Even today, that rich tradition continues.

units.name: Mesa Verde National Park
units.description: For over 700 years, the Ancestral Pueblo people built thriving communities on the mesas and in the cliffs of Mesa Verde. Today, the park protects the rich cultural heritage of 27 Pueblos and Tribes and offers visitors a spectacular window into the past. This World Heritage Site and International Dark Sky Park is home to over a thousand species, including several that live nowhere else on earth.

units.name: Mount Rainier National Park
units.description: Ascending to 14,410 feet above sea level, Mount Rainier stands as an icon in the Washington landscape. An active volcano, Mount Rainier is the most glaciated peak in the contiguous U.S.A., spawning five major rivers. Subalpine wildflower meadows ring the icy volcano while ancient forest cloaks Mount Rainier’s lower slopes. Wildlife abounds in the park’s ecosystems. A lifetime of discovery awaits.

units.name: New River Gorge National Park and Preserve
units.description: A rugged, whitewater river flowing northward through deep canyons, the New River is among the oldest rivers on the continent. The park encompasses over 70,000 acres of land along the New River, is rich in cultural and natural history, and offers an abundance of scenic and recreational opportunities.

attractions.name: Endless Wall Trail
attractions.description: A forest walk crosses Fern Creek and follows the gorge rim to cliffside views, including Diamond Point. The published trail distance excludes the road walk needed to return between its two trailheads.

length.method: NPS Length field: "2.4 miles/3.86 km (One-way)". Trail distance only; the separately described road return is excluded. No conversion or doubling.

attractions.name: Long Point Trail
attractions.description: The trail crosses fields and forest before a steeper final approach to a rock outcrop overlooking the gorge and New River Gorge Bridge. The viewpoint has unprotected cliff edges.

conflicts.detail: The individual page pairs 1.6 miles with 1.29 km for a one-way distance; the units disagree.

attractions.name: Sandstone Falls Boardwalk
attractions.description: Bridges and boardwalks connect river islands and viewing decks beside Sandstone Falls. The route passes a riverside flatrock plant community associated with powerful Appalachian rivers.
attractions.accessibility: NPS describes the boardwalk as accessible; it crosses bridges to islands and observation decks.

conflicts.detail: The individual page gives 0.2 miles one way and describes 0.25 mile; no numeric length has been selected.

history.event: New River Gorge became a National Park System unit as New River Gorge National River.
New River Gorge National River was redesignated New River Gorge National Park and Preserve under Public Law 116-260.

Help steward the ecological heart of the Cascades.

Come explore!

units.name: Petrified Forest National Park
units.description: A landscape where deep time lies fully on display, Petrified Forest National Park blends colorful badlands, vast grasslands, and one of the world’s largest and most vivid collections of petrified wood. Spanning more than 200 million years of geologic history, the park protects ancient fossils, ancestral Puebloan sites, habitat for desert animals, and a sweeping stretch of historic Route 66.

units.name: Redwood National Park
units.description: Renowned for the world’s tallest trees, Redwood’s landscapes span from open prairies and oak woodlands to pristine rivers and untamed coastline. This ancient home has supported people for thousands of years. The National Park Service and California State Parks now work to safeguard and rejuvenate these lands for everyone’s enjoyment, learning, and inspiration.

units.name: Saguaro National Park
units.description: Tucson, Arizona is home to the nation's largest cacti. The giant saguaro is the universal symbol of the American west. Here you have a chance to see these enormous cacti, silhouetted by the beauty of a magnificent desert sunset.

units.description: When Theodore Roosevelt came to Dakota Territory to hunt bison in 1883, he was a skinny, young, spectacled dude from New York. He could not have imagined how his adventure in this remote and unfamiliar place would forever alter the course of the nation. The rugged landscape and strenuous life that TR experienced here would help shape a conservation policy that we still benefit from today.

units.name: Wind Cave National Park
units.description: Wind Cave National Park protects two very different worlds - one deep within the earth, the other a sunlit world of many resources. Bison, elk, and other wildlife roam the rolling prairie grasslands and forested hillsides of one of America's oldest national parks. Below the remnant island of intact prairie sits Wind Cave, one of the longest and most complex caves in the world.

attractions.name: Prairie Vista
attractions.description: Waysides interpret prairie grasslands on a loop starting near the visitor center.

attractions.name: Elk Mountain
attractions.description: A campground loop follows the meeting of grassland and forest; elk bugling may be heard in autumn.

attractions.name: Rankin Ridge
attractions.description: A nature loop reaches the park's highest point and distant views; the fire tower itself is closed.

attractions.name: Wind Cave Canyon
attractions.description: A former road follows limestone cliffs and forested hillsides toward the park boundary.

attractions.name: Cold Brook Canyon
attractions.description: Ponderosa forest gives way to prairie and a prairie-dog town along the canyon.

conflicts.detail: Numeric length withheld: inconsistent miles and kilometres. See the official guide; no correction or conversion was imposed.

attractions.name: Lookout Point
attractions.description: Rolling prairie descends toward Beaver Creek and connects to longer loop options.

attractions.name: East Bison Flats
attractions.description: A steep climb from Wind Cave Canyon leads into rolling prairie and views of Buffalo Gap and the Black Hills.

attractions.name: Sanctuary
attractions.description: Rolling prairie and a large prairie-dog town lead toward the Highland Creek junction.

attractions.name: Centennial
attractions.description: This park segment forms part of the much longer Black Hills Centennial Trail, crossing prairie, pine forest and Beaver Creek.

attractions.name: Highland Creek
attractions.description: The park's longest trail crosses mixed-grass prairie, ponderosa forest and riparian habitats.

attractions.name: Boland Ridge
attractions.description: A succession of climbs affords Black Hills, Red Valley and prairie panoramas.

units.name: Yosemite National Park
units.description: Not just a great valley, but a shrine to human foresight, the strength of granite, the power of glaciers, the persistence of life, and the tranquility of the High Sierra. First protected in 1864, Yosemite National Park is best known for its waterfalls, but within its nearly 1,200 square miles, you can find deep valleys, grand meadows, ancient giant sequoias, a vast wilderness area, and much more.

attractions.name: Lower Yosemite Fall Trail
attractions.description: A paved circuit approaches the base of Lower Yosemite Fall and offers views of the falls and Yosemite Creek. Spray is strongest during high spring and early summer flows.
attractions.accessibility: The eastern portion of the paved loop is wheelchair accessible when free of ice and snow; this statement does not apply to the entire loop.

attractions.name: Cook's Meadow Loop
attractions.description: Paths and boardwalks cross the Yosemite Valley meadow landscape, with views of Yosemite Falls, Half Dome, Glacier Point, and Sentinel Rock. The circuit includes road crossings.
attractions.accessibility: NPS describes the trail as wheelchair accessible when not covered in snow. Boardwalks can be slippery when wet or frosted.

attractions.name: Mirror Lake Trail (lake and back)
attractions.description: The shorter Mirror Lake outing follows a paved service road to the lake below Tenaya Canyon. Water is usually fullest in spring and early summer; the separate longer circuit continues beyond the paved section.

length.method: NPS Trail Overview: "Distance: 2 miles (3.2 km) round trip to lake and back". The lake-and-back option only, excluding the separately listed five-mile loop.

history.event: President Abraham Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant, setting aside Yosemite Valley and the Mariposa Grove for public use and recreation under California's administration.
An Act of Congress established Yosemite National Park.
Yosemite Valley and the Mariposa Grove were transferred from California to the federal government and included in Yosemite National Park.

units.name: Zion National Park
units.description: Follow the paths where people have walked for thousands of years. Gaze up at massive sandstone cliffs of cream, pink, and red that soar into a brilliant blue sky. Experience the tall, stretching walls of a narrow slot canyon. Zion’s unique array of plants and animals will enchant you as you absorb the rich history of the past and enjoy the excitement of present-day adventures.

attractions.name: Zion Nature Center
attractions.description: Details and accessibility information for the Zion Nature Center, which opens seasonally during the summer.

attractions.name: Watchman Trail
attractions.description: From the Zion Canyon Visitor Center, the trail follows the river before climbing sandy, rocky terrain to a viewpoint over lower Zion Canyon and Springdale. There are drop-offs along the route.

length.method: NPS Duration text: "Watchman trail is 3.3 miles (5.3 km) roundtrip." Published whole-hike distance; not derived from the separately assessed overlook and loop segments.

attractions.accessibility: The unpaved route is sandy, rocky, and uneven, with drop-offs. NPS assesses the approach and overlook loop as separate segments with steps and steep grades.

attractions.name: Riverside Walk
attractions.description: A paved path follows the Virgin River from the Temple of Sinawava into narrowing sandstone walls. It reaches the beginning of The Narrows; entering the river is a separate continuation.
attractions.accessibility: Paving is irregular in places, minor drop-offs occur, and sand can make the concrete slippery. NPS reports steep sections; paving alone does not establish wheelchair suitability for the whole route.

conflicts.detail: The accessibility survey gives 1 mile one way; the spring 2026 guide gives 2.2 miles round trip.

attractions.name: Pa'rus Trail
attractions.description: The main trail connects Zion Canyon Visitor Center with Canyon Junction along the Virgin River, offering Watchman views and interpretive exhibits. It is shared with bicycles and leashed pets.
attractions.accessibility: NPS describes the main route as wheelchair accessible. The optional unpaved connector to the Human History Museum is not designed for wheelchairs.

conflicts.detail: The individual page describes 3.5 miles end-to-end and 1.6 miles one way in its survey; the spring 2026 guide labels 3.5 miles round trip.

history.event: A presidential proclamation established Mukuntuweap National Monument, protecting the area that became Zion National Park.
The monument was enlarged and renamed Zion National Monument.
An Act of Congress established Zion National Park.

units.name: Natchez Trace Parkway
units.description: The Natchez Trace Parkway is a 444-mile recreational road and scenic drive through three states. It roughly follows the "Old Natchez Trace," a historic travel corridor used by American Indians, "Kaintucks," European settlers, slave traders, soldiers, and future presidents. Today, people can enjoy a scenic drive as well as hiking, biking, horseback riding, and camping along the Parkway.

units.name: Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve
units.description: Tallgrass prairie once covered 170 million acres of North America, but within a generation most of it had been transformed into farms, cities, and towns. Today less than 4% remains intact, mostly in the Kansas Flint Hills. Established on November 12, 1996, the preserve protects a nationally significant remnant of the once vast tallgrass prairie ecosystem. Here the tallgrass makes its last stand.

units.name: Valles Caldera National Preserve
units.description: About 1.2 million years ago, a spectacular volcanic eruption created a 14-mile-wide circular depression in the earth now known as Valles Caldera. The preserve is known for its huge mountain meadows, abundant wildlife, and meandering streams. The area also preserves the homeland of ancestral native peoples and embraces a rich ranching history.

attractions.name: History Grove
attractions.description: History Grove is one of the only old growth ponderosa pine forests in New Mexico.

units.name: Amistad National Recreation Area
units.description: An oasis in the desert, Amistad National Recreation Area consists of the US portion of the International Amistad Reservoir. Amistad, a Spanish word meaning "friendship," is known for excellent water-based recreation, camping, hiking, and rich cultural history dating back nearly 5,000 years. Amistad is also home to a wide variety of plant and animal life both above and below the water.

units.name: Bighorn Canyon National Recreation Area
units.description: The vast, wild landscape of Bighorn Canyon National Recreation Area offers visitors unparalleled opportunities to immerse themselves in the natural world, and experience the wonders of this extraordinary place. With over 120,000 acres, one can find an astounding diversity in ecosystems, wildlife, and more than 10,000 years of human history to explore.

attractions.name: Beaver Pond Nature Trail
attractions.description: Yucca flats and a ridge above Lime Kiln Creek lead down a steep hillside to beaver ponds and evidence of dam-building.

attractions.name: Bighorn Head Gate
attractions.description: A gravel path reaches remnants of an early-twentieth-century irrigation system. Water levels can submerge the head gate.

attractions.name: Three Mile Access
attractions.description: A riverside path follows the Bighorn River to a cottonwood grove, with opportunities to observe fishing and waterbirds.

attractions.name: Visitor Center Pond
attractions.description: A concrete loop behind the Lovell visitor center circles a former solar-reflection pond now returning toward marsh habitat.

attractions.name: Sykes Mountain Trail
attractions.description: A rugged desert-mountain ascent reaches overlooks of Bighorn Canyon and Horseshoe Bend; summer heat is a particular concern.

attractions.name: Mouth of the Canyon Trail
attractions.description: Views of the Pryor and Bighorn Mountains contrast with red Chugwater outcrops near Horseshoe Bend.

attractions.name: State Line Trail
attractions.description: Juniper scrubland and limestone plateaus lead to a canyon-rim view, with a connection toward Ranger Delight.

attractions.name: Ranger Delight
attractions.description: A faint road cut and saddle lead toward the canyon rim from near the Montana state line.

attractions.name: Sullivan's Knob Trail
attractions.description: A canyon-rim walk passes near the ancient Bad Pass Trail, seasonally used by Indigenous travelers between the Bighorn Basin and Northern Plains.

attractions.name: Two Eagles Interpretive Trail
attractions.description: Interpretation explains stone circles left by Indigenous families who weighted tipi edges with stones. These cultural resources must remain in place.

attractions.name: Lower Layout Creek Trail
attractions.description: An old two-track road follows the area south of Layout Creek, with views into Layout Creek Canyon.

attractions.name: Upper Layout Creek Trail
attractions.description: A steep hike explores Layout Creek’s water and ranching landscape, whose irrigation history includes Erastus Ewing’s 1897 water claim.

attractions.name: Barry's Island Trail
attractions.description: A former two-track road circles Chain Canyon, once used by cattle rustlers, toward Barry’s Island; high reservoir water may cover parts of the route.

units.name: Boston Harbor Islands National Recreation Area
units.description: With 34 islands and peninsulas, the Boston Harbor Islands offer numerous opportunities for visitors to explore, enjoy, and find respite. View historic lighthouses, explore tide pools, hike lush trails, camp under the stars, or relax while fishing, picnicking, or swimming—all within reach of downtown Boston. Composed of eleven agencies, the Boston Harbor Islands Partnership stewards the islands to ensure their open access and preservation for future generations.

units.name: Lake Meredith National Recreation Area
units.description: Set within the wide‑open Texas Plains, Lake Meredith National Recreation Area offers a peaceful retreat in the heart of rugged grasslands. These quiet coves sustain an unexpectedly rich array of life, providing seven distinct habitats.

units.name: Lake Roosevelt National Recreation Area
units.description: The ancient geologic landscape of the upper Columbia River cradles Lake Roosevelt in walls of stone carved by massive ice age floods. Swim, boat, hike, camp, and fish at this hidden gem in Northeast Washington, created by the Grand Coulee Dam.

units.name: Ozark National Scenic Riverways
units.description: Ozark National Scenic Riverways is the first national park area to protect a river system. The Current and Jacks Fork rivers are two of the finest floating rivers found anywhere. Spring-fed, cold and clear: they are a delight to canoe, swim, boat, or fish. units.name: Great Egg Harbor National Scenic and Recreational River

The 129-mile river system flows through Pinelands National Reserve.

Today, the Obed stretches along the Cumberland Plateau and offers visitors a variety of outdoor recreational opportunities.

Explore sandy beaches, salt marshes, maritime forests and coastal bays. Rest, relax, recreate and enjoy some time on the edge of the continent.

units.name: Canaveral National Seashore
units.description: Discover a dynamic barrier island shaped by dunes, coastal hammocks, and Mosquito Lagoon. Walk among ancient Timucua shell mounds and connect with thousands of years of human history. Immerse yourself in a protected sanctuary where diverse plants and wildlife thrive—making Canaveral National Seashore a place where nature, history, and discovery come together.

units.name: Cape Cod National Seashore
units.description: The great Outer Beach described by Thoreau in the 1800s is protected within the national seashore. Forty miles of pristine sandy beach, marshes, ponds, and uplands support diverse species. Lighthouses, cultural landscapes, and wild cranberry bogs offer a glimpse of Cape Cod's past and continuing ways of life. Swimming beaches and walking and biking trails beckon today's visitors.

units.name: Cape Hatteras National Seashore
units.description: The sound of ocean waves, the starry night sky, or the calm of the salt marshes, you can experience it all. Shaped by the forces of water, wind, and storms these islands are ever changing. The plants, wildlife, and people who live here adapt continually. Whether you are enjoying the beach, kayaking the sound, or climbing the Cape Hatteras Lighthouse there is something for everyone to explore!

units.name: Cape Lookout National Seashore
units.description: A boat ride three miles off-shore brings you to the barrier islands of Cape Lookout National Seashore. Horse watching, shelling, fishing, birding, camping, lighthouse climbing, and touring historic villages--there’s something for everyone at Cape Lookout. Be sure to bring all the food, water, and supplies you need (and carry your trash out of the park) when visiting these remote beaches.

units.name: Cumberland Island National Seashore
units.description: St Marys is the gateway to Cumberland Island, Georgia's largest and southernmost barrier island. Here pristine maritime forests, undeveloped beaches and wide marshes whisper the stories of both man and nature. Natives, missionaries, enslaved African Americans and Wealthy Industrialists all walked here. Cumberland Island is also home to over 9,800 acres of Congressionally designated Wilderness.

units.name: Fire Island National Seashore
units.description: Immerse yourself in an enchanting collage of coastal life and history. Rhythmic waves, high dunes, ancient maritime forests, historic landmarks and glimpses of wildlife, Fire Island has been a special place for diverse plants, animals and people for centuries. Far from the pressure of nearby big-city life, dynamic barrier island beaches offer solitude, camaraderie, and spiritual renewal.

units.name: Padre Island National Seashore
units.description: Protecting sixty-six miles of wild coastline along the Gulf of America, the narrow barrier island is home to one of the last intact coastal prairie habitats in the United States. Along the hypersaline Laguna Madre, tidal mud flats teem with life. Native Americans, Spanish explorers and cattle ranchers have walked along its shores. Padre Island National Seashore is waiting to be rediscovered.

units.name: Point Reyes National Seashore
units.description: From its thunderous ocean breakers crashing against rocky headlands and expansive sand beaches to its open grasslands, brushy hillsides, and forested ridges, Point Reyes offers visitors over 1500 species of plants and animals to discover. Home to several cultures over thousands of years, the Seashore preserves a tapestry of stories and interactions of people. Point Reyes awaits your exploration.

units.name: Prince William Forest Park
units.description: Prince William Forest Park is an oasis, a respite of quiet and calm. In 1936, Chopawamsic Recreation Area opened its gates to house children's 'relief' camps during the Great Depression. Renamed Prince William Forest Park in 1948, these fragrant woods and trickling streams have welcomed generations of campers, hikers, bikers and nature lovers. Discover Northern Virginia's best kept secret!

units.name: Rock Creek Park
units.description: Rock Creek Park is truly a gem in our nation's capital. This 1,754 acre city park was officially authorized in 1890, making it the third national park to be designated by the federal government. It offers visitors the opportunity to escape the bustle of the city and find a peaceful refuge, recreation, fresh air, majestic trees, wild animals, and thousands of years of human history.

As one of the most iconic sites in the country, the White House and President's Park seeks to tell the stories of all people who have lived, worked, and visited.

units.description: The Chicago Portage preserves a remnant of the overland link between the Great Lakes and Mississippi River systems. Indigenous travelers used this route before Marquette and Joliet crossed it in 1673. Forest Preserves of Cook County maintains the wooded landscape and interpretation near Lyons, Illinois; it is separately classified as an affiliated area.

units.description: Green Springs National Historic Landmark District in Virginia’s Piedmont encompasses over 14,000 acres. Many of the farmsteads, often dating to the 19th century and connecting to one another visually, are preserved through easements.

units.name: Inupiat Heritage Center
units.description: On the rooftop of the world, the Iñupiat Heritage Center in Barrow, Alaska, tells the story of the Iñupiat people. They have thrived for thousands of years in one of the most extreme climates on Earth, hunting the bowhead, or "Agviq." In the 19th century, the quiet northern seas swarmed with commercial whalemen from New England, who also sought the bowhead for its valuable baleen and blubber.

units.name: Thomas Cole National Historic Site
units.description: In 1825, America was still a new nation, just forming its own unique identity and traditions. Thomas Cole invented a new style of art, one that Americans could call their own. His landscape paintings launched the art movement known as the Hudson River School. His groundbreaking achievements took place here in Catskill, New York -- in the "peaceful shades" of his beloved home, Cedar Grove.

units.name: Touro Synagogue National Historic Site
units.description: Touro Synagogue, a building of exquisite beauty and design, steeped in history and ideals, and one of the most historically significant Jewish buildings in America, was designated a National Historic Site in 1946. Dedicated in 1763, it still serves an active congregation and each year greets over 30,000 visitors who come to see the magnificent interior and hear its remarkable story.
